Volume 11 · Chapter 07

Stress testing and risk aggregation

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v11-c06

By the endBuild internally consistent stress scenarios without double counting exposures.

Volume 11 · Chapter 7

Reconcile stressed values with executable payments

A stress report can overstate a loss by charging a default twice and understate a funding need by counting collateral twice. It can also produce a perfectly correct number for an incoherent scenario. The remedy is an exposure inventory, a common clock, explicit payment rights and a calculation that can be reconciled from beginning to end.

Capability. Construct joint stress scenarios, revalue nonlinear claims, trace their effects through equity and executable payments, solve a small contagion mechanism, and certify a reverse-stress boundary. Distinguish that conditional calculation from a probability estimate or an institutional permission to take risk.

Prerequisites. Use bank accounting and incentives from Chapter 1, asset/capital distinctions from Chapter 2, joint-loss reasoning from Chapter 4, dated funding and collateral from Chapter 5, and execution/model-control limits from Chapter 6. Discounting and finite proofs use Volumes 2 and 10. All institutions, prices, scenarios and contracts below are original synthetic constructions.

1. A scenario is a joint conditional statement

A stress scenario specifies a coherent set of conditions and asks what follows for a defined institution and horizon. A sensitivity changes a particular assumption; a reverse stress starts with an adverse outcome and searches a stated set of conditions that produces it. None supplies a probability merely by being severe. The largest loss among five chosen scenarios is not a 99% quantile without a justified joint probability law and adequate support.

The BCBS’s final October 2018 principles motivate clear objectives, internally consistent scenarios, material-risk coverage, usable data, interactions between solvency and liquidity, and independent challenge. They are high-level international guidelines, not a national rule or a calibration for this exercise. Our finite mechanisms and proofs are developed here.

Fix the legal entity, currency, valuation time, payment cutoff, exposure identifiers, seniority, netting rights and measurement conventions before aggregating. A consolidated group total does not make cash transferable between subsidiaries. A promised facility is different from one drawable before the cutoff. Future management actions need prices, quantities, timing and counterparties; labels such as “deleveraging” do not execute transactions.

We study institution I in one currency unit, CU. Marks change at today’s opening stress instant. An operational cash incident then occurs; a specified network batch settles; I draws available secured funding; an old secured creditor receives its required principal paydown; deposit withdrawals are served last. All these events occur in that order before today’s cutoff. Secured principal and one day’s interest are due tomorrow. A borrower pays in one year and a bond in two years. Those later asset receipts are not available today or tomorrow.

For the teaching measurement, scenario changes in asset values enter current profit and equity; deposits and secured principal remain at contractual principal. This is an explicitly chosen stress balance sheet, not a complete fair-value accounting system, a regulatory capital measure or an assertion about an accounting standard. Today has no elapsed funding-interest accrual; tomorrow’s specified interest is reported separately. The calculation stops at today’s cutoff and reports later obligations without claiming that refinancing them has been demonstrated.

2. Revalue the same claims once

I’s opening inventory, before the stress
ItemContract / dateOpening amount, CU
CashAvailable in I’s account now12
Zero-coupon bond110.25 in two years; reference yield 5%100
Borrower claim84 in one year; reference yield 5%80
Claim on network B10 in today’s clearing batch10
Deposits137 outstanding; scenario specifies today’s requests137 liability
Old secured funding20 principal; 25% of the bond inventory reserved20 liability
Equity202 assets less 157 liabilities45

The network claim is a different contract from I’s borrower claim. The borrower and B/C’s external obligors are stipulated to share an industrial stress factor; there is no duplicate ownership of one receivable. This factor-sensitive credit cluster has opening value 80+10=90, or 45/101 of assets. Two legal debtor names do not establish independent risks. The bond and borrower claim also share the scenario yield, so their rate exposure overlaps even though their cash-flow maturities differ.

Let y be the scenario annual yield with 1+y>0, d∈[0, 1] the fraction of the borrower’s promised cash lost, and RB the actual network receipt. The stipulated marks are

P(y)=110.25/(1+y)²; Q(y, d)=84(1−d)/(1+y).
Lbond=100−P; Lloan=80−Q; Lnetwork=10−RB.
E=45−Lbond−Lloan−Lnetwork−o,

where o is the cash incident loss. These are conditional scenario prices/cash assumptions, not probabilities inferred from a discount rate. Bond revaluation is nonlinear: P′(y)=−220.5/(1+y)³ and P″(y)=661.5/(1+y)⁴>0. At y=.05, duration linearization gives ΔP≈−(200/1.05)Δy. A .10 increase predicts a loss of 19.047619, whereas exact revaluation loses 16.635161. Convexity accounts for the direction of the approximation error; a larger shock requires the full price.

Credit and rate effects interact on the same borrower claim. One exact attribution first changes the yield, then reduces cash at that new yield:

80−84(1−d)/(1+y) = [80−84/(1+y)] + 84 d/(1+y).

Using 80 d for the second term while also using the new-yield rate loss changes the attribution. At y=.15, d=.20 the exact loan loss is 21.565217: 6.956522 rate loss plus 14.608696 credit increment. Using the reference-yield credit amount 16 would overstate the sum by 1.391304. Adding a further “default loss” to the already complete 80−Q would count the same cash-flow impairment again. An alternative ordering of attribution can be valid, but the total must reconcile.

3. A complete small contagion mechanism

External institutions B and C each owe T=20 in today’s batch. B owes fraction a=1/2 to C and the rest to I; C owes fraction a to B and the rest to an outside household sector. All obligations have the same priority within each payer. Available external cash is b for B and c for C. No other assets, borrowing, bankruptcy costs or guarantees are available by the cutoff. Limited liability caps total payments by available resources; each creditor receives its promised fraction of the payment. Retained excess belongs to the payer’s equity holders.

The batch permits incoming interbank funds to support outgoing payments simultaneously. This is an assumed enforceable clearing arrangement, not a model of sequential gross settlement with intraday funding bottlenecks. I has no outgoing obligation to B/C in this batch. Consequently I receives RB=(1−a)pB, where total payments solve

pB=min (T, b+apC),   pC=min (T, c+apB).

Existence and uniqueness for 0≤a<1. The map sends the closed square [0, T]² into itself. Because min (T, z) is 1-Lipschitz, distances in the maximum norm shrink by at most a. Starting at any point, successive differences are bounded by a geometric sequence; the remaining difference after k steps is at most ak‖p1−p0‖/(1−a). Thus the iterates are Cauchy in the closed square. Their limit exists and continuity makes it a fixed point. If two fixed points existed, their distance would be at most a times itself, forcing equality. This proves the needed result, rather than presuming that a numerical loop’s stopping tolerance defines a payment rule.

The model solves exactly by checking four candidates: (T, T), (b+aT, T), (T, c+aT), and ((b+ac)/(1−a²), (c+ab)/(1−a²)). Every fixed point belongs to a regime where each payment is capped or below its cap. Substitution tests which candidate satisfies both equations. At regime boundaries candidates may coincide; uniqueness concerns the payment vector, not the number of regime labels.

Resources and comparative statics. Retained amounts are eB=b+apC−pB≥0 and eC=c+apB−pC≥0. Adding yields

b+c=(1−a)pB+(1−a)pC+eB+eC.

Internal receipts cancel: summing them again as external resources would create money in the stress report. Starting iteration at zero also shows that increasing either external resource weakly increases both payments. For two resource vectors, the fixed-point equations imply ‖p−p̃‖≤‖(b, c)−(b̃, c̃)‖/(1−a), proving continuity. These properties will support reverse stress. A closed cycle at a=1 is different: with b=c=0 every (p, p), 0≤p≤T, satisfies the equations. Our lab caps a at .75 and does not claim uniqueness outside its domain.

Worked example 2: loss transmitted through the other bank

At b=c=12, both pay 20; each retains 2 and each outside creditor receives 10. At b=2, c=8, both payments are below 20, so pB=2+pC/2 and pC=8+pB/2. Substitution gives pB=8, pC=12. I receives 4; the other outside creditor receives 6; retained cash is zero. External cash 2+8 equals 4+6 exactly.

If one incorrectly holds C’s payment at its full 20, B would pay 12 and I would receive 6. I’s standalone loss would be 4; the simultaneous solution instead loses 6. The extra 2 is a feedback effect transmitted through the contracted payment network. It is not another loss to add after the claim has already been marked from 10 to 4. The loss of 6 contains that effect.

4. An equity loss is not every cash movement

The original quarter of the bond remains reserved for the old secured creditor even after paydown. With haircut h its capacity is (1−h)P/4. The required principal reduction is M=max (20−(1−h)P/4, 0). The distinct unpledged three-quarters can support a new draw of at most D̄=min (F, (1−h)3 P/4). The facility is stipulated to remain drawable up to F under the given row’s conditions; no unstated material-adverse-change covenant is silently waived. A real application needs evidence for that availability.

After the cash incident and network receipt, cash is A=12−o+RB. To pay M and withdrawal request w while retaining the chosen reserve m=2, the smallest planned draw is D*=max (M+w+m−A, 0). Actual drawing is D=min (D*, D̄). The new pledged fraction D/[(1−h)P] is no larger than 3/4. The original quarter is never reused.

The fixed priority is explicit: pay min (A+D, M) to the old creditor, then pay the smaller of remaining cash and w to depositors. Unpaid principal or withdrawal requests remain owed. No negative-cash transaction is posted, and a missed margin requirement is reported rather than presumed harmless. Acceleration, resolution and subsequent default costs would require an extended contract. The signed budget A+D̄−M−w is maximum cash after all requested payments; if negative, it is a shortage certificate, not an actual negative cash balance.

New borrowing adds equal cash and debt. Old principal paydown reduces both. A deposit payment reduces cash and deposits. Pledging assets changes encumbrance, not asset ownership. None automatically reduces profit or equity. A future sale at the already recorded mark also does not repeat the earlier mark loss. A sale below that mark, a fee, an interest charge or a new default cost would require its own additional amount and date.

Worked example 3: fund the transactions that can actually occur

In joint stress, P=44100/529≈83.364839. Old-pool capacity is P/8≈10.420605, so M=10135/1058≈9.579395. The new collateral could support 33075/1058≈31.261815, but the facility ceiling is only 20. Cash after the incident and clearing is 12−2+4=14. Retaining 2 after paying everything would require 37.579395 of new funding. Draw 20, giving cash 34; pay the old creditor 9.579395; pay depositors the remaining 24.420605. The unfilled deposit request is 15.579395 and actual cash is zero.

Closing deposits are 137−24.420605=112.579395. Old secured principal is 10.420605 and new principal 20. Assets are bond 83.364839 plus loan 58.434783, totaling 141.799622; liabilities total 143. Equity is −1.200378, exactly the independently calculated stress loss result. The network claim has been replaced by its cash receipt and is no longer an asset. This reconciles both the shortage and the negative equity without treating the 49.579395 requested principal/deposit payments as an expense.

The new pledge is 1058/2205 of the original bond inventory, alongside the original quarter. Next-day secured principal is 30.420605; at the stipulated daily rate .001, interest is .030421 and total payment 30.451026. The borrower’s stressed cash 67.2 arrives in one year and the bond’s 110.25 in two. The report has not shown how tomorrow’s payment is financed.

In the funding outage, all marks are unchanged and equity is 45. The network pays 10, cash becomes 22, no new facility is operationally available, and depositors request 30. Pay 22 and leave 8 owed. The unpledged bond still has value, but no sale or other facility is assumed executable before the cutoff. The outage is a payment failure with positive equity.

5. Aggregate state-consistent losses, then take a maximum

For component losses Lj(s) measured on the same exposures, date and accounting basis, total loss in scenario s is their sum. Across a common finite scenario set S,

maxs∈S ΣjLj(s) ≤ Σj maxs∈SLj(s).

For any fixed s, every component is no greater than its own maximum; sum and then maximize to prove the inequality. Equality requires compatible maximizers, or an equivalent attaining combination. Independence is neither assumed nor needed for this deterministic statement. Component maxima from different narratives do not automatically define an admissible common scenario.

Our bond maximum is 8800/529≈16.635161, the loan maximum is 520/17≈30.588235, and the network and incident maxima are 6 and 2. Their sum is 496624/8993≈55.223396. The actual largest total among the five rows is joint stress, 24440/529≈46.200378. The gap is 3528/391≈9.023018. The sum combines the rate-rise bond loss with the more severe recession credit haircut, even though that row has a bond gain. This is an upper bound for this menu, not a discovered joint scenario, a probability-weighted risk measure or a guarantee against omitted scenarios.

Aggregation also requires a perimeter. B-to-C and C-to-B flows cancel when assessing their combined external resources, but I’s claim on B remains an exposure for I alone. A group cannot add a subsidiary’s equity impairment and the same underlying asset impairment twice in a consolidated asset-loss total. Conversely, eliminating an internal position for accounting consolidation does not make legal-entity payment bottlenecks disappear.

6. Reverse stress with a valid boundary

Specify the search family before asking for its weakest shock. For x∈[0, 1], set y=.05+.10 x, d=.20 x, b=12−10 x, c=12−4 x, h=.20+.30 x, w=20+20 x and o=2 x, with the facility ceiling fixed at 20. This family is distinct from the five-row menu; in particular it does not contain the funding outage. Its severity coordinate is not a probability or a distance measured in historical standard deviations.

Management chooses a capital threshold e=10 and reserve threshold m=2. Define capital slack K(x)=E(x)−10 and funding-capacity slack H(x)=A(x)+D̄(x)−M(x)−w(x)−2. The intervention trigger is K≤0 or H≤0. Funding capacity uses all available new drawing, not the minimum-draw policy’s chosen closing balance. Reference closing cash is already 2, but it still has 20 of unused facility headroom and H(0)=20.

Boundary proof. Along this family bond value and borrower value are continuous and nonincreasing; the network resource monotonicity and continuity proved above give the same properties for RB. The cash incident and withdrawals do not decrease. Collateral capacity cannot increase, and old margin required cannot decrease. Therefore K, H and φ=min (K, H) are continuous and nonincreasing. The trigger set {x∈[0, 1]:φ(x)≤0} is closed in a compact interval. If nonempty it has a minimum. If φ(0)≤0 the reference already triggers; if φ(1)>0 there is no trigger in this supported family. Otherwise a safe lower point and triggering upper point bracket the first boundary.

Bisection preserves φ(lower)>0 and φ(upper)≤0, replacing one endpoint according to the midpoint sign. After n steps the width is 2−n; continuity and monotonicity place the minimum within the bracket even if the function has a flat segment. Do not return a midpoint as a certified exact root. The lab returns rational endpoints and both slacks, uses 40 steps here, and distinguishes an absent boundary from an already-triggered reference.

Worked example 4: the first trigger is loss of funding headroom

Network payments along the family can be solved without repeated numerical iteration:

pB(x)=20 for 0≤x≤1/5;
pB(x)=22−10 x for 1/5≤x≤1/3;
pB(x)=24−16 x for 1/3≤x≤1.
pC(x)=20 until x=1/3, then 24−12 x.

The two boundaries lie above 1/3, where RB=12−8 x. Put z=1.05+.10 x. The free collateral supports at least 31.261815 throughout, so the fixed ceiling 20 binds potential new drawing. Old margin is positive for x>0. Capital and reserve boundary equations reduce to the following cubics after multiplying by z²>0:

GK(x)=110.25+84(1−.20 x)z−(143+10 x)z²=0.
GH(x)=(2−30 x)z²+110.25(.20−.075 x)=0.

Independent polynomial evaluation agrees with the full balance-sheet bisection. The reserve boundary is approximately .545784230258; the capital boundary is .751688814506. Each stored bracket has width 2−40≈9.095×10−13. At the first boundary equity is approximately 19.650135, above 10, and the institution can still make every requested payment while retaining 2. It has exhausted the modeled funding headroom beyond that reserve. This is the chosen intervention point, not a claim that a payment has already been missed.

With the reserve floor changed to zero, zero maximum cash occurs at about .596675093210. Actual nonpayment begins strictly beyond that point. Thus the infimum severity of strict payment failure need not itself be a failure. A closed policy trigger at equality avoids confusing an attained minimum with the open condition “shortage>0.” None of these boundaries searches other causal paths such as the separate outage.

7. What the calculation leaves for judgment

Payment feedback in B/C and I’s draw decision are endogenous to the specified contracts. Yield, haircut, external resources and facility access are exogenous scenario inputs. If many banks respond by selling the same asset, the fixed price may cease to be consistent with sale volumes. A fire-sale extension needs an explicit demand/price rule, holdings, collateral remargining and a solution concept. Adding an unspecified “contagion multiplier” would obscure those resource constraints. Likewise, changing a policy changes the reverse-stress problem; the old threshold need not survive a new covenant, asset sale, queue priority or capital raise.

For institutional use, challenge the driver narrative, omitted exposures, cash-flow mapping, collateral eligibility, operational cutoffs, legal rights and management actions. Document which facts are observed, which quantities are estimated and which assumptions are hypothetical. Retain a reproducible exposure-to-result trail and show decision makers both the results and the limitations. The response may be more capital, timely cash, smaller concentrated exposures, a changed contract or an escalation; each intervention requires its own funded scenario calculation.

Download the synthetic inputs, model, exact output, manifest and standalone instructions. Run python3 v11-c07-analysis.py --input v11-c07-inputs.json --output result.json. The quiet run(data) API returns JSON-compatible rational strings without mutating data. Python’s standard library suffices. The bounded domain, partial-payment policy, future-date limits and explicit normal/optimized error behavior are documented in the README. Exact arithmetic certifies this synthetic calculation; it does not validate the contracts or the scenario’s likelihood.

8. Exercises

  1. Revaluation and attribution. Recompute the rate-rise row’s bond, loan, total loss and equity. Derive the bond’s first-order loss for the .10 yield increase and compare with exact loss. For joint stress, reconcile the loan’s loss by changing the rate first and credit second. Quantify the error from using reference-yield credit loss 80 d in that decomposition.
  2. Clearing proof and transfer. Prove the two-node map has a unique fixed point for 0≤a<1, and prove the external-resource identity. With T=20, a=1/2, b=4, c=6 find both payments, I’s receipt, I’s total impairment and the feedback loss relative to assuming C pays 20. Give a counterexample to uniqueness at a=1.
  3. Funding and collateral. Reconstruct every joint-stress funding movement and closing balance-sheet total. Then raise the contractual and available new facility ceiling to 40, changing nothing else in that row. Calculate actual collateral capacity, drawing, unpaid withdrawals and total pledged fraction. Does the larger facility remove the capital loss or make all requested payments possible?
  4. One receivable, one impairment. In sector recession the network claim begins at 10, is marked to 4 and then pays 4. Show its income and balance-sheet entries. Explain the errors in also charging 6 when the cash arrives, treating the old secured paydown as an expense, or treating a later bond sale at its already recorded mark as another mark loss. State an additional event that would create a genuine further loss.
  5. Aggregation and concentration. Prove the finite-menu maximum inequality. Compute the four component maxima, their sum, the actual largest common-scenario loss and their gap. Explain why neither independence nor a 99% interpretation follows. Calculate the opening industrial credit-cluster share and identify two distinct ways an apparent diversification claim could fail.
  6. Reverse-stress certificate. Derive the piecewise network payments on the stated x family and both cubic equations above. Explain why the first boundary is attained and why 40 bisections certify it. Report both approximate boundaries, the capital position at the first one, and the distinction between the reserve trigger and strict payment failure. Explain why an outage outside the family does not contradict the boundary proof.
  7. Funded intervention. Before the opening snapshot, inject 5 of external cash as new equity. Keep today’s withdrawal requests and every other scenario driver fixed. Recompute opening equity and both reverse boundaries. Repeat when the same 5 cash is instead funded by a new deposit liability. Explain why the funding improvement can be the same while the capital improvement differs, and what omitted behavioral response would invalidate this comparison.
  8. Committee memo and research critique. A report calls the largest five-row loss a 99% stress quantile, adds an extra network feedback loss to the marked claim, assumes every bank can sell its collateral at the same fixed price, and treats positive future asset receipts as tomorrow’s funding. Correct all four claims. Propose one exposure/data check, one independent model check and one contractual/execution check, each with a limitation. Give a decision response to the outage without inventing a usable facility, and state the evidence needed before assigning scenario probabilities.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. At y=.15, P=110.25/1.15²=44100/529≈83.364839 and Q=84/1.15=1680/23≈73.043478. Bond and loan losses sum to 12480/529≈23.591682; the network and incident losses are zero. Equity is 45−12480/529≈21.408318. Since P′(.05)=−200/1.05=−4000/21, the first-order loss is 400/21≈19.047619, exceeding the exact 8800/529≈16.635161 by 2.412458. Convexity implies the tangent price is below the actual price.

    In joint stress Q=67.2/1.15=1344/23≈58.434783. Total loan loss is 496/23≈21.565217. Rate-first loss is 160/23≈6.956522 and credit increment is 336/23≈14.608696. Reference credit loss 16 instead gives 528/23≈22.956522; the excess is 32/23≈1.391304. The altered denominator caused the mismatch; it is not an extra cash-flow loss.

  2. The map is a self-map of [0, T]² with maximum-norm Lipschitz constant a. Geometric bounds on successive iterates make them Cauchy, continuity gives a fixed point, and ‖p−q‖≤a‖p−q‖ forces any two fixed points to coincide. Nonnegative retained resources eB=b+apC−pB and eC=c+apB−pC sum to b+c−(1−a)(pB+pC), proving the identity. This relies on the specified simultaneous batch and pari passu shares.

    For b 4, c 6, neither cap binds. Solve pB−pC/2=4 and pC−pB/2=6 to obtain 28/3 and 32/3. I receives 14/3; impairment is 10−14/3=16/3. Holding C’s payment at 20 would give I 7, so feedback adds 7−14/3=7/3 of loss within the total 16/3. Outside receipts 14/3+16/3 exhaust the 10 external cash. At a 1, b=c 0, every (p, p) in the square is fixed; the strict contraction hypothesis matters.

  3. After the incident and receipt, cash is 14. Required old paydown is 10135/1058≈9.579395; the facility caps drawing at 20. Draw to cash 34, pay old principal, then pay depositors 25837/1058≈24.420605, leaving 16483/1058≈15.579395 unpaid and cash 0. Closing deposits are 119109/1058≈112.579395, old secured principal 11025/1058≈10.420605 and new principal 20. Their sum is 143. Bond plus loan assets are 75012/529≈141.799622; equity −635/529≈−1.200378 reconciles.

    With ceiling 40, free collateral still caps drawing at 33075/1058≈31.261815. Cash 14 plus this draw less old paydown funds 18876/529≈35.682420 of withdrawals. Unpaid requests are 2284/529≈4.317580. The new pledge uses the full three-quarters; with the original quarter, the total is 1. Equity loss is unchanged because borrowing and principal payments are not expenses. Neither all payments nor solvency is restored by increasing a ceiling beyond usable collateral.

  4. Write down the claim by 6 and equity/current stress profit by 6; the claim is then 4. Settlement adds cash 4 and removes claim 4, with no further income effect. Charging another 6 records the same impairment twice. Old principal paydown reduces cash and debt equally. A sale at the recorded mark replaces the bond asset with equal cash. These movements alter liquidity or funding composition without creating another loss. A sale below the mark, a transaction fee, a newly worsened recovery, an actual interest expense or a separately specified default cost could create an incremental loss; the relevant amount, right and date must be stated.

  5. For every s and j, Lj(s)≤maxtLj(t); summing and maximizing establishes the inequality. Maxima are 8800/529, 520/17, 6, 2. Their sum 496624/8993≈55.223396 exceeds the common-row maximum 24440/529≈46.200378 by 3528/391≈9.023018. Different rows attain different components. There is no assigned probability law, hence no independence assumption or identified 99% quantile. The industrial credit share is 90/202=45/101≈44.5545%. Distinct debtors can share a cash-generating factor; an interbank claim can transmit the other institution’s exposure through its payment links. Common rate sensitivity is a further overlapping factor. Counting names alone resolves none of these mechanisms.

C then has 12−4 x+(22−10 x)/2=23−9 x, at least 20 exactly until x=1/3. Thereafter solving the two linear equations gives pB=24−16 x and pC=24−12 x, with the adjacent expressions agreeing at both boundaries.

    For x≥1/3, RB=12−8 x, so E=P+Q −133−10 x and K=P+Q −143−10 x. Multiplication by z² gives GK. Along this family the minimum free collateral capacity is its endpoint 31.261815>20. For x>0 old paydown is 20−(.8−.3 x)P/4. Substitution gives H=2−30 x+(.2−.075 x)P, and multiplying by z² gives GH. Both slacks are positive at 1/3, so roots found above that point do not miss an earlier trigger.

    Continuity and monotonicity make the nonempty closed trigger set in [0, 1] have an attained minimum. Exact bisection maintains a strictly safe lower endpoint and a triggering upper endpoint with width 2−40. The funding boundary is about .545784230258, where equity is 19.650135; the capital boundary is about .751688814506. All requested payments remain possible at the first boundary, with maximum remaining cash 2. At zero reserve floor the zero-cash boundary is about .596675093210; strict shortages occur only beyond it. The proof searches only the declared one-dimensional family. The separate outage changes facility access and is outside that set, so its failure is compatible with the result.

  7. An external equity infusion makes opening cash 17, assets 207, liabilities 157 and equity 50. Scenario marks and incident losses are unchanged, so every capital slack rises 5; funding-capacity slack also rises 5. The new funding boundary is approximately .673395979956 and the capital boundary .861274373503. Funding still triggers first.

    A new deposit of 5 instead gives assets 207, deposits 142, secured principal 20 and equity 45. With the requested withdrawals deliberately held fixed, usable cash and hence funding slack rise by the same 5; the funding boundary remains .673395979956. Capital slack does not change and its boundary remains .751688814506. The deposit adds a claim on future resources rather than net worth. If those depositors withdraw during the stress, demand a different interest rate, or alter confidence/other withdrawals, the frozen-demand comparison fails and the liability cash-flow model must be changed. Neither intervention’s cash may be counted until actually received before the opening snapshot.

  8. Illustrative response. The largest row is a conditional menu maximum, not a quantile. The claim’s mark from 10 to 4 already includes network feedback; an extra charge duplicates part of that loss. Common fixed sale prices require a market-depth or demand assumption consistent with total proposed sales. Future asset receipts do not establish timely cash or collateral monetization at tomorrow’s deadline.

    Reconcile contract identifiers, balances and counterparties to the exposure inventory, including internal eliminations and off-balance commitments; a clean reconciliation does not verify scenario severity. Independently solve the network/resource certificates and perturb the rate-credit and collateral mappings; agreement checks implementation but not true external resource behavior. Verify facility terms, custody, eligibility and actual settlement capability with a dated operational test; success in one drill cannot guarantee access in every crisis. For the outage, record 8 unpaid, escalate and obtain a specifically executable timely funding or payment-agreement response; do not insert an uncommitted facility into cash. Assigning probabilities requires a defended joint data-generating model, available information, uncertainty treatment and validation beyond the stress menu; severe hypothetical paths may remain useful without assigned likelihoods.

    Rubric, 12 points: one for each of four corrected claims; one each for the three concrete checks with limitations; two for the reconciled shortage and conditional executable response; two for probability evidence and uncertainty; one for distinguishing model evidence from authority to approve risk. Double counting a marked impairment, spending future cash before its date, or inventing available borrowing requires correction regardless of the total score.

9. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In three minutes explain why the joint-stress loss, cash shortage and reverse-stress threshold answer different questions. Include one network equation and one funding entry.

Model response. The stress loss 46.200378 reduces opening equity 45 to −1.200378. It includes the network claim’s loss 6: pB=2+pC/2 and pC=8+pB/2 solve to 8 and 12, so I receives 4. Drawing 20 adds cash and secured debt; it does not reverse that loss. After old principal paydown, deposit withdrawals remain short 15.579395. The reverse boundary .545784230258 belongs to a separate prescribed severity family and a reserve-headroom trigger; at that point payments still occur and equity remains 19.650135. It is not a run probability or the weakest conceivable path to default.

Delayed check, one week later. (1) Why can reference actual closing cash 2 coexist with positive funding headroom? (2) Which network hypothesis supplies uniqueness? (3) Does a 4 receipt after a 10-to 4 mark create another 6 loss? (4) Does a larger facility ceiling eliminate a collateral cap? (5) Is the strict-shortage boundary necessarily an actual shortage? (6) Can five scenario rows identify a 99% quantile?

Answers. (1) The minimum-draw policy leaves unused facility capacity 20; the reverse measure uses maximum feasible cash, not chosen cash. (2) External shares make a<1 and the clearing map a contraction; a closed a=1 cycle can be nonunique. (3) No: remove the 4 claim and add 4 cash. (4) No: joint free collateral supports only 31.261815 at that haircut. (5) No: zero shortage may hold at the infimum of positive shortages; our intervention trigger includes equality. (6) No probability law or tail-support claim follows from that menu. Revisit Sections 3–4 for clearing/cash, Section 5 for common-scenario aggregation and Section 6 for reverse-stress hypotheses.

Next steps. Chapter 8 applies dated obligations and common-shock reasoning to insurance, pensions and household finance. Later systemic-risk work can extend the explicitly small network and endogenize prices and policy responses. Those extensions require additional contracts and evidence, not larger labels on this calculation.
